data: Roscosmos / Lavochkin Association (lead spacecraft) — Soviet Academy of Sciences instruments

~4400 kg combined: flyby bus + 760 kg titanium descent capsule (cameras, X-ray fluorescence soil-composition spectrometer, seismometer, soil-sampling arm with hermetic-vault drill). Designed for one of the most hostile descent environments ever attempted.

© Roscosmos / Lavochkin / IKI / NASA NSSDCA archive. Venera 13 launched 1981-10-30 from Baikonur. After a 122-day cruise the descent capsule separated and braked through Venus's atmosphere using parachutes, then a final aero-brake disc; it landed 1982-03-01 at 7.5°S 303°E in the Phoebe Regio highlands. Surface conditions at touchdown: 457 °C, 89 atm, sulfuric-acid haze. Venera 13 survived 127 minutes — the longest surface survival of any Venus mission, beating its design target by about 95 minutes. During that window it returned the first colour panoramic images of another planet's surface (two 180° colour panoramas), recorded the first audio from another planet's surface via wind-microphone, and used its drill + onboard XRF to determine that the landing site basalt was a weakly differentiated leucite alkaline composition. Twin spacecraft Venera 14 (launched 1981-11-04, landed 1982-03-05) performed nearly identical operations at a different site. The Venera series — Venera 4 through 16 (1967-1983) — remains the only successful surface program at Venus to date.

Baikonur Cosmodrome, 1981-10-30. Soviet Venus mission carrying a lander designed to survive Venus's 460°C, 90-bar surface environment. Venera 13 + 14 are twin spacecraft launched 5 days apart; both landed successfully.

Soft-landed 1982-03-01 at Phoebe Regio. Transmitted for 127 minutes from the surface — about four times its 32-minute design life — and returned the first colour panoramic images of Venus's surface, sampled the soil with an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer, and recorded the first audio from the surface of another planet (wind on Venus's microphone). The lander succumbed to the heat after ~2 hours.
Longest surface survival of any Venus mission (127 min); first colour panoramic images and first audio from another planet's surface

The peak of the Soviet Venera program. Venera 13 launched 1981-10-30 and landed 1982-03-01 at 7.5°S 303°E in the Phoebe Regio highlands. Surface conditions at touchdown: 457 °C, 89 atm, sulfuric-acid haze. The lander survived 127 minutes — about four times its 32-minute design life — returning the first colour panoramas from another planet's surface, recording wind microphone audio, and using its drill + onboard X-ray fluorescence spectrometer to determine that the basalt at the landing site was a weakly differentiated leucite alkaline composition. Twin spacecraft Venera 14 performed identical operations at a separate site five days later. The Venera series (1967–1983) remains the only successful surface program at Venus to date.
Proton-K / D-1 lifts Venera 13 from Baikonur on a 122-day cruise.
